title: Inspect the tables and establish the grain
scenario: Before analysing any healthcare dataset, establish what each row represents and how many records are available.
task: Return the row count and distinct key count for both tables. Identify the grain of each table in one sentence.
requirements: Return row_count and distinct_key_count for encounters.
Return row_count and distinct_key_count for medication_orders.
Do not assume that the two row counts represent the same unit.
starter:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT encounter_id) AS distinct_key_count
FROM encounters;

-- Repeat for medication_orders using order_id.
hint: The encounter table has one row per encounter. The medication table has one row per order.
solution:
SELECT 'encounters' AS table_name,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       COUNT(DISTINCT encounter_id) AS distinct_key_count
FROM encounters
UNION ALL
SELECT 'medication_orders', COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
FROM medication_orders;
expected: encounters: 80 rows / 80 unique encounter IDs. medication_orders: 150 rows / 150 unique order IDs.
check: Both keys are unique in this teaching dataset. A different result would require investigating duplicate records or the declared grain.

title: Filter a defined reporting period
scenario: The operations team requests encounters admitted during the first quarter of 2026.
task: Return encounter ID, admission date, department and length of stay for admissions from 1 January through 31 March 2026, ordered from newest to oldest.
requirements: Use an inclusive start date and exclusive next-period boundary.
Return only the four requested columns.
Sort by admission_date descending, then encounter_id.
starter:
SELECT encounter_id, admission_date, department, length_of_stay_days
FROM encounters
WHERE admission_date >= '2026-01-01'
  AND admission_date < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY admission_date DESC, encounter_id;
hint: ISO-formatted YYYY-MM-DD text sorts chronologically. An exclusive upper bound avoids time-of-day edge cases if the field later becomes a timestamp.
solution:
SELECT encounter_id, admission_date, department, length_of_stay_days
FROM encounters
WHERE admission_date >= '2026-01-01'
  AND admission_date < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY admission_date DESC, encounter_id;
expected: 80 rows. All supplied encounter admissions fall between 2026-01-01 and 2026-03-31.
check: Confirm the minimum and maximum admission dates with MIN and MAX. Do not use an unbounded year filter if the requested period is a quarter.

title: Build department-level operational metrics
scenario: A department manager wants encounter volume and mean length of stay by department.
task: Return one row per department with encounter_count and mean_los_days rounded to two decimals.
requirements: Use encounter-level data only.
Sort by encounter_count descending and department ascending.
Label the mean in days.
starter:
SELECT department,
       COUNT(*) AS encounter_count,
       ROUND(AVG(length_of_stay_days), 2) AS mean_los_days
FROM encounters
GROUP BY department;
hint: Because encounters is one row per encounter, COUNT(*) is the encounter count in this dataset. This would not be safe after joining to medication_orders.
solution:
SELECT department,
       COUNT(*) AS encounter_count,
       ROUND(AVG(length_of_stay_days), 2) AS mean_los_days
FROM encounters
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY encounter_count DESC, department;
expected: Emergency 24 / 3.75 days; General Medicine 15 / 3.60; Cardiology 14 / 4.21; Orthopaedics 14 / 4.21; Neurology 13 / 3.69.
check: Department encounter counts must sum to 80. The mean is descriptive and does not explain why LOS differs.

title: Find therapeutic classes with high order volume
scenario: The pharmacy analytics team wants classes with at least 20 medication-order records.
task: Count orders by therapeutic class and return only classes with 20 or more orders.
requirements: Use medication_orders only.
Count order records, not unique patients or administrations.
Sort by order_count descending.
starter:
SELECT therapeutic_class, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM medication_orders
GROUP BY therapeutic_class
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20;
hint: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
solution:
SELECT therapeutic_class, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM medication_orders
GROUP BY therapeutic_class
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20
ORDER BY order_count DESC, therapeutic_class;
expected: Calcium-channel blocker 27; Statin 25; ACE inhibitor 23; ARB 21; Antidiabetic 21. (Ties may be sorted alphabetically.)
check: The sum of all therapeutic-class counts must equal 150.

title: Join encounters to medication orders safely
scenario: A clinical analytics colleague asks for order counts by department.
task: Return department and medication_order_count, counting orders assigned to encounters in each department.
requirements: Join on encounter_id.
Use clear aliases.
Do not call the output encounter count.
starter:
SELECT e.department, COUNT(*) AS medication_order_count
FROM encounters e
JOIN medication_orders m
  ON e.encounter_id = m.encounter_id
GROUP BY e.department;
hint: The joined table has one row per matching medication order, not one row per encounter. COUNT(*) is correct here only because the requested measure is order count.
solution:
SELECT e.department,
       COUNT(m.order_id) AS medication_order_count
FROM encounters e
INNER JOIN medication_orders m
  ON e.encounter_id = m.encounter_id
GROUP BY e.department
ORDER BY medication_order_count DESC, e.department;
expected: Order counts by department: Emergency 52; Neurology 27; Orthopaedics 26; General Medicine 24; Cardiology 21.
check: The department order counts must sum to 150. If asked for encounter count instead, use COUNT(DISTINCT e.encounter_id) or aggregate at encounter grain first.

title: Measure encounter coverage with LEFT JOIN
scenario: The team wants to know how many encounters have at least one medication order and how many have none.
task: Return each department's total encounters, encounters with at least one order, and encounters with no orders.
requirements: Preserve encounters with no matching orders.
Avoid multiplying encounter rows in the output.
Use a pre-aggregated order table or COUNT(DISTINCT).
starter:
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT encounter_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM medication_orders
  GROUP BY encounter_id
)
SELECT ...
hint: Aggregate the many-side table to one row per encounter before joining. LEFT JOIN keeps encounter records without orders.
solution:
WITH order_counts AS (
  SELECT encounter_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM medication_orders
  GROUP BY encounter_id
)
SELECT e.department,
       COUNT(*) AS total_encounters,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) > 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS encounters_with_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS encounters_without_orders
FROM encounters e
LEFT JOIN order_counts o ON e.encounter_id = o.encounter_id
GROUP BY e.department
ORDER BY e.department;
expected: The total_encounters column sums to 80. encounters_with_orders sums to 70; encounters_without_orders sums to 10.
check: For every department, with_orders + without_orders must equal total_encounters. The LEFT JOIN is essential to retain zero-order encounters.

title: Create an encounter-level medication summary
scenario: A quality analyst needs a dataset with one row per encounter and its number of medication orders.
task: Create a CTE that aggregates orders by encounter, then join it to encounters. Return encounter ID, department, LOS and order_count, including encounters with zero orders.
requirements: Final output must contain exactly 80 rows.
Keep one row per encounter.
Use COALESCE to represent no matching order records as zero.
starter:
WITH orders_per_encounter AS (
  SELECT encounter_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM medication_orders
  GROUP BY encounter_id
)
SELECT ...
hint: The CTE collapses the many-side table to at most one row per encounter before the join.
solution:
WITH orders_per_encounter AS (
  SELECT encounter_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM medication_orders
  GROUP BY encounter_id
)
SELECT e.encounter_id, e.department, e.length_of_stay_days,
       COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) AS order_count
FROM encounters e
LEFT JOIN orders_per_encounter o
  ON e.encounter_id = o.encounter_id
ORDER BY e.encounter_id;
expected: 80 rows. Sum of order_count is 150; 10 encounters have order_count = 0.
check: Run SELECT COUNT(*) over the CTE result or wrap this query in a subquery. If it returns more than 80 rows, the many-side aggregation or join key is wrong.

title: Rank departments by mean length of stay
scenario: The operations director wants departments ranked by mean length of stay, retaining tied ranks.
task: Return department, encounter_count, mean_los_days and rank, with highest mean LOS ranked first.
requirements: Aggregate to one row per department first.
Use DENSE_RANK so ties share a rank.
Do not rank individual encounters.
starter:
WITH dept_metrics AS (
  SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS encounter_count,
         AVG(length_of_stay_days) AS mean_los
  FROM encounters GROUP BY department
)
SELECT ...
hint: A window function operates over the already aggregated department rows. Do not use a window rank directly over raw encounter rows for this task.
solution:
WITH dept_metrics AS (
  SELECT department,
         COUNT(*) AS encounter_count,
         AVG(length_of_stay_days) AS mean_los
  FROM encounters
  GROUP BY department
)
SELECT department, encounter_count,
       ROUND(mean_los, 2) AS mean_los_days,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY mean_los DESC) AS los_rank
FROM dept_metrics
ORDER BY los_rank, department;
expected: Cardiology and Orthopaedics tie at 4.21 days and share rank 1. Emergency is 3.75; Neurology 3.69; General Medicine 3.60.
check: The rank is a descriptive ordering, not a performance judgement. Consider case mix, sample size and clinical context before interpreting differences.

title: Calculate the supplied 30-day flag proportion
scenario: A quality team asks for the proportion of encounters marked with the supplied readmission flag.
task: Calculate total encounters, flagged encounters and flagged proportion as a percentage. Clearly label this as a supplied synthetic flag.
requirements: Use encounters as the unit of analysis.
Make numerator and denominator visible.
Do not call it a validated readmission rate.
starter:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_encounters,
       SUM(CASE WHEN readmission_30d_flag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS flagged_encounters,
       ... AS flagged_percent
FROM encounters;
hint: Multiply numerator / denominator by 100.0 to avoid integer division. Protect against a zero denominator with NULLIF.
solution:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_encounters,
       SUM(CASE WHEN readmission_30d_flag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS flagged_encounters,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN readmission_30d_flag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
             / NULLIF(COUNT(*), 0), 2) AS supplied_flag_percent
FROM encounters;
expected: 80 total encounters; 7 flagged encounters; 8.75% supplied-flag proportion.
check: The flag's derivation, eligibility criteria and 30-day follow-up completeness are not validated. This is not a standardised hospital readmission metric.

title: Run key, chronology and referential-integrity checks
scenario: Before publishing a report, run basic data-quality checks on keys, dates and foreign-key relationships.
task: Write queries that identify duplicate encounter IDs, duplicate order IDs, discharge dates before admission dates, and medication orders referencing missing encounters.
requirements: Each check must return the number of violating records.
A zero result means no issue was found by that specific check.
Do not silently delete or repair invalid records.
hint: For chronology, compare ISO date strings using discharge_date < admission_date. For orphan orders, use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL.
expected: All four checks return 0 on the current synthetic dataset.
check: A passing check only means the tested rule passed. It does not establish overall data quality, clinical validity or completeness.

title: Inspect a query plan and justify an index
scenario: A recurring report filters medication orders by therapeutic class and status. You need to explain how SQLite accesses the table.
task: Inspect the query plan for a class/status filter. Compare the plan before and after creating an index on (therapeutic_class, order_status).
requirements: Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
Create an index only in your local practice database.
Explain the trade-off: faster reads can add storage and write overhead.
starter:
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT order_id, order_date, drug_name
FROM medication_orders
WHERE therapeutic_class = 'Statin'
  AND order_status = 'Active';
hint: SQLite may choose a table scan for a small table even when an index exists. The planner's choice depends on table size, statistics and selectivity.
solution:
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_orders_class_status
ON medication_orders(therapeutic_class, order_status);

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT order_id, order_date, drug_name
FROM medication_orders
WHERE therapeutic_class = 'Statin'
  AND order_status = 'Active';
expected: A valid plan is returned. The current Academy database already contains idx_orders_class_status. The planner may still choose a scan because the dataset is small.
check: Do not claim an index improved performance unless you measured it on representative data. Index design should follow real query patterns and production workload.
